Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
The event happened because of the way I acted

vignette: Anna is a 26-year-old firefighter whose uniform still carries the ash of the day she was trapped inside a collapsed warehouse during a wild-fire rescue. The day began with the roar of sirens and a frantic march of hoses toward the building, but when the structure gave way she found herself suffocating in a narrow crawl space, the only light coming from emergency lamps. The crack of splintering wood, the rush of wind, and the pounding of her own heart followed her into a twelve-hour night in a hospital bed with a bandaged leg and a mind that refuses to rest. The memory of that day is a photograph in Anna's mind: a vivid, photographic recall that feels more real than any other memory she has. It is alien, as if someone else had lived it, and each time she sees a photo of herself in uniform, the image slides into the present, forcing her to relive the suffocation and the sense that she had lost her agency. That image itself is a trigger-old photographs of her at the scene bring the memory back in a flash. The crowded emergency rooms she once entered now seem threatening; the very sense of crowding at the firehouse after shift feels like the walls closing in on her, and her thoughts spiral into self-blame, as if her own actions had precipitated the collapse. That self-blame also keeps the memory vivid, making her feel as if she is still inside the collapse, and it intensifies her perception of threat. Because of that guilt, Anna feels that she has lost part of herself. She tells herself that if she had not moved in that direction during the collapse, the building would have collapsed later or a colleague would have been injured. That belief, rooted in self-blame, turns ordinary sounds into alarms: even the hum of the kitchen exhaust at the fire station can trigger a racing heartbeat and a surge of the remembered suffocation, pulling her into that nightmarish space. The sudden intrusions of the memory during such sounds become flashbacks, and each flashback feels as real as the day itself. The vivid recall of the suffocation makes her hear any noise as a possible threat, a threat that is always present. The constant fear has turned ordinary sounds into alarms. The more often she is startled, the more the images of the collapsed building flood her thoughts; the more those images come to life, the more her self-blame grows louder. The more she anticipates danger, the more she feels the event is personal, and the memory feeds that sense. The more that threat is felt, the more she avoids the very things that used to bring her joy. She no longer looks at old photographs; she keeps her phone face down in her locker. The crowded shift-meetings feel like an impending collapse, so she sits at the back and keeps her distance from the firehouse's social gatherings, fearing that the crowd will trigger the next flashback. Anna's avoidance has begun to affect her work. She misses out on advanced training sessions because the thought of a crowded room sends her heart racing. When a teammate offers to discuss a new rescue technique, she shrugs, convinced that the conversation will lead to a trigger that will bring her back to the suffocation. She also avoids talking to her partner about her feelings, fearing that expressing vulnerability will be perceived as weakness and may cause her to be held accountable for future incidents. The weight of the memory, the persistent threat, and the self-critical thoughts have made her feel isolated from her team and uncertain about her identity as a firefighter. She has reached a point where she can no longer sleep at night without the sound of her own breathing sounding like the creak of a collapsing wall. The daily startle, the flashbacks, the constant inability to relax even in safe spaces have become unbearable. That night, after watching a colleague laugh loudly at a joke, she felt the memory surge with such intensity that she could not stay awake. In the morning she made the decision to seek professional help, hoping to regain the sense of self she feels she has lost and to find a way to calm the startle that has hijacked her life. Her biggest fear is that the cycle will never end, but she clings to the hope that talking about it might finally let the images step out of her mind.
